sources.title: R. H. Dana, The Seaman’s Friend, fifth edition (1847)
sources.excerpt: Moving the rudder from a right line has the effect of deadening the ship’s way.
sources.fact: Headway matters to the rudder. Tacking puts the bow through the wind; wearing turns away through a longer arc. Backed sails can also turn a slow vessel.

sources.title: A. T. Mahan, The Influence of Sea Power upon History (1890)
sources.excerpt: the power of giving or refusing battle at will
sources.fact: The weather gage offers tactical initiative, but bearing down can sacrifice broadside fire and expose the approaching vessel to raking. It does not guarantee victory.

sources.title: Collingwood’s Trafalgar dispatch, 22 October 1805
sources.locator: London Gazette 15858, 6 November 1805; On Monday / Action began
sources.excerpt: Wind about West, and very light
sources.fact: The British bore up in two columns against the northward-headed enemy line. Close action followed the passage through that line.

sources.title: Royal Museums Greenwich, Queen Charlotte breaking the line, PAD8695
sources.locator: Collection description, Glorious First of June
sources.excerpt: tacked round to engage them with her starboard broadside
sources.fact: The description distinguishes crossing the line, changing tack, and bringing the starboard broadside to bear; its interpretation says “appears”, and the sketch is not a measured track.

sources.title: Richmond Weed, The Battle of the Virginia Capes, Proceedings (1940)
sources.locator: Discussion of the NNE wind and diverging lines
sources.excerpt: The vans of the two fleets were closer than their rears.
sources.fact: The two fleets’ forward divisions were closer than their rear divisions. Rear ships maintaining station could be beyond useful gun range.

sources.title: USS Constitution Museum, Escaping a British Squadron, 17–19 July 1812
sources.locator: Calm, towing / kedging, and the later squall
sources.fact: Calm impeded the chase; boats and anchors supplied movement, and later weather and sail handling affected the escape.

sources.title: US Navy historical image NH 42907: Shannon and Chesapeake, 1 June 1813
sources.excerpt: Captain Broke ordered the ships to be lashed together
sources.fact: Close parallel firing preceded entanglement and securing the ships, then boarding across their contact. The caption’s claim about an unattended helm is conjecture.

sources.title: US Navy Ordnance Instructions, fourth edition (1866)
sources.fact: Preparation, grapnels, designated passages, an explicit assault order and resistance are distinct. Defenders can deny a foothold. This later manual includes steam-era equipment and supplies no universal bridge dimensions or deployment time.

sources.title: Broke’s official report, 6 June 1813, London Gazette 16750
sources.locator: 10 July 1813, printed pp. 1329–1330; original page scans
sources.excerpt: gave orders to prepare for boarding
sources.fact: Rigging entanglement preceded the ordered assault; resistance continued from the decks, tops and below before quarter and prize management. The letter does not itself say that the ships were lashed together.

sources.title: Bainbridge’s Java engagement journal, USS Constitution Museum 2361.1
sources.locator: Five-page transcript of the secretarial official copy; PDF pp. 2–4
sources.excerpt: Our wheel was shot entirely away
sources.fact: Wheel, rudder-chain and rigging damage did not instantly stop all maneuver. Apparent surrender was checked, and a boat and officer took possession. Emergency steering and independent damage systems remain outside this harness.

sources.title: Charles Morris’s autobiography, Proceedings, April 1880
sources.locator: Philadelphia operation: rope approach, securing the ketch, chain plates and forward hatchways
sources.excerpt: secure the ketch to the ship
sources.fact: Boats connected ropes, crews hauled the vessels together, and an assigned party secured the source craft. Climbing and internal hatch routes were physical passages. This participant memoir was published posthumously, decades after the action.

sources.title: Hamilton’s Hermione report, 1 November 1799, London Gazette 15223
sources.locator: Printed pp. 61–62; original issue headed 18–21 January 1800, Admiralty item dated 21 January
sources.excerpt: the Main-Deck held out much longer
sources.fact: Forecastle, quarter-deck, main-deck and lower resistance were distinct; cutting cables, making sail and towing occurred during the struggle. It gives no standardized locked-door breach time or durability.

Health, fitting durability, cabin capacity and costs come from current game definitions. Ordinary damage and deaths remain enabled.
Local mechanism slice: Hermione was attacked from boats. These two game hulls, five personnel and an RTS gangway do not recreate its boats, ratings or historical timing.
Both hulls retain ordinary HP and cabin parts; their guns are removed to measure infantry resistance. The carrier passenger-output balance rule remains active.

One defender enters the cabin through the ordinary command before the recorded battle. Cabin breach means the game loses shelter and tries the hatch route; this is not evidence that Hermione had a timed destructible locked door.
No historical winner is prescribed. Control cannot transfer while a living original defender remains aboard, including in the cabin; surrender and prisoner management are not modeled.
